stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. In the Route 53 public hosted zone, app.example.com is an A record that holds the IP addresses of the load balancer. An engineer copied the addresses when the load balancer was created. Users now report intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks. The company wants to stop the errors. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: holds the IP addresses of the load balancer
intermittent connection errors, mostly after traffic peaks

options.text: Replace the A record with a CNAME record for app.example.com whose value is the DNS name that AWS assigned to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: It works, because the name follows the load balancer, but Route 53 [charges for CNAME queries](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-queries-free-cname-charged), so it costs more than an alias record.

options.text: Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that reads the current load balancer addresses every minute and writes them into the A record for app.example.com.
options.why: The function adds cost, and resolvers keep the old addresses [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) after each rewrite.
options.misconception: believes that rewriting the record every minute keeps every user on the current addresses

options.text: Associate Elastic IP addresses with the Application Load Balancer, and replace the values of the A record for app.example.com with those Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: Elastic IP addresses do not attach to an Application Load Balancer: in the feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) belongs to the [Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only).

options.text: Replace the A record with an alias record of type A for app.example.com that points to the Application Load Balancer.
options.why: Route 53 follows the address changes of the load balancer for an alias record, and Amazon Route 53 [doesn't charge for alias queries to ELB](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-elb-no-query-charge) load balancers.

explanation: Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer and updates its DNS entry with a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-elb-dns-entry-updated-ttl-60), so copied addresses go stale after peaks. With an alias record, [Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-follows-resource-ip-changes) and answers with the current addresses.
takeaway: Point a name at a load balancer with an alias record: Route 53 follows its changing addresses at no query charge.
twin: If the stem said "app.example.com must point to a host name of a partner outside AWS" instead: a CNAME record, because an alias record [can only redirect queries to selected AWS resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-targets-only-selected-aws-resources).

stem: A company runs the same stateless web application in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. The application has users around the world. The company hosts its DNS records in a Route 53 public hosted zone. Each user must be served from the Region that gives that user the lowest latency. Which routing configuration for www.example.com will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Each user must be served from the Region that gives that user the lowest latency

options.text: Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record in each Region, with Evaluate Target Health turned on for both records.
options.why: Route 53 uses [latency data taken over a period of time](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-changes-over-time) and answers with the record of the Region that is fastest for that user.

options.text: Geolocation alias records: a Europe record that points to the eu-west-1 load balancer, and a Default record for the us-east-1 load balancer.
options.why: Geolocation routing uses the [geographic location of the requests](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-geo-vs-latency-geography-not-latency), and in some cases geography is not a good proxy for latency.

options.text: Weighted alias records for the two load balancers with equal weights, so that each Region receives half of the DNS queries for the name.
options.why: Weights split queries among [multiple resources in proportions that you specify](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions), whatever the location of the user, so half of the users reach the slower Region.
options.misconception: believes that equal weights send each user to the nearer Region

options.text: IP-based records with a CIDR collection that the team keeps current with the client IP ranges that each of the two Regions must serve.
options.why: It can work, but the team maintains the client IP ranges by hand; IP-based routing suits users [from certain ISPs to specific endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-ip-based-routing-use-cases).

explanation: The requirement names latency, not a place. Latency records send each user to [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region), with no list of networks to maintain. Evaluate Target Health lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) if one Region fails.
takeaway: Lowest latency for each user means latency records; a rule about places means geolocation records.
twin: If the stem said "Because of a data residency rule, users in Europe must be served from eu-west-1, and all other users from us-east-1" instead: geolocation records, because each user location [always goes to the same endpoint](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-use-cases).

stem: A company will migrate www.example.com from web servers in its data center to an Application Load Balancer next Saturday. In the Route 53 public hosted zone, www.example.com is an A record with a TTL of 86,400 seconds. Users must move to the new site with minimal downtime, and the team must be able to roll back quickly if the new site fails. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST downtime for users?

options.text: On Saturday, replace the A record with an alias record for the load balancer, because Route 53 sends record changes to all of its servers within a minute.
options.why: Route 53 updates its own servers [within 60 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-propagation-within-60-seconds), but resolvers keep the old answer until the TTL of 86,400 seconds runs out.

options.text: Two days before Saturday, lower the TTL of the A record to 300 seconds; on Saturday, replace the record with an alias record for the load balancer.
options.why: AWS suggests a shorter TTL, [such as 300 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-ttl-start-shorter-300-seconds-in-use), for a name in use; after two days the short TTL is in every cache.

options.text: On Saturday, lower the TTL of the A record to 300 seconds and replace it with an alias record for the load balancer in the same change.
options.why: Resolvers that cached the old answer keep it for the old TTL of 86,400 seconds, so a lower TTL set on Saturday comes too late.
options.misconception: believes that resolvers drop a cached answer when the TTL of the record is lowered

options.text: Create a second public hosted zone for example.com with an alias record for the load balancer, and change the name servers at the registrar on Saturday.
options.why: Resolvers cache NS records too, with a typical TTL of [172800 seconds](../facts/route53.md#route53-ns-record-typical-ttl-172800), so a change of name servers moves users more slowly.
options.misconception: believes that a change of name servers reaches users faster than a record change

explanation: Resolvers cache an answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so after a change some users keep the old address for up to 86,400 seconds. Lower the TTL first, as AWS advises: [temporarily shorten the TTLs](../facts/route53.md#route53-best-practice-shorten-ttl-before-critical-change). After two days every cache holds the short TTL, so the switch and a roll back reach users within minutes.
takeaway: Lower the TTL before a planned DNS change, and wait for the old TTL to pass before the switch.
twin: If the stem said "an A record with a TTL of 60 seconds" instead: change the record on Saturday, because resolvers cache the old answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control).

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the approach with the LEAST downtime for users.
I mark the constraints: the A record has a TTL of 86,400 seconds, the move is next Saturday, and the team must be able to roll back quickly.
Before I look at the options, I predict that the TTL must go down days before the move, because resolvers keep a cached answer until its TTL runs out.

I remove the change on Saturday alone, because Route 53 updates its own servers fast, but resolvers keep the old answer for up to a day. I remove the second hosted zone, because resolvers also cache NS records, typically for two days.

Between lowering the TTL two days early and lowering it on Saturday, the difference is when the caches learn the short TTL; the stem says minimal downtime, so the short TTL must be in every cache before Saturday.
Check: lowering the TTL two days early meets every constraint, and a roll back also reaches users within minutes. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company serves www.example.com from three Amazon EC2 instances that have Elastic IP addresses. Route 53 answers with three weighted A records, each with a nonzero weight and its own health check. During a failed deployment, all three instances failed their health checks, but users still received the addresses of the failed instances. When no instance is healthy, users must see a static error page from an S3 bucket named www.example.com that is configured as a website. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: each with a nonzero weight and its own health check
users still received the addresses of the failed instances

options.text: Rename the three weighted records, then create failover records for www.example.com: an alias record for the weighted records as the primary, and the S3 website as the secondary.
options.why: It works, because the primary alias record stays healthy as long as [at least one of the weighted records](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-evaluate-target-health-weighted-branch) is healthy, but it adds a renamed tree and two records.

options.text: Lower the TTL of the three weighted records to 60 seconds, so that resolvers drop the failed addresses soon after Route 53 stops returning the unhealthy records.
options.why: When no record is healthy, Route 53 [considers all the records in the group](../facts/route53.md#route53-no-record-healthy-all-records-considered-healthy) healthy and keeps returning them, so no error page appears.

options.text: Add a fourth weighted record for www.example.com: an alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0, and keep the three records as they are.
options.why: Route 53 first uses [only the nonzero weighted records](../facts/route53.md#route53-weighted-zero-weight-health-nonzero-first); when all of them are unhealthy, it [considers the zero-weighted records](../facts/route53.md#route53-weighted-zero-weight-used-when-all-unhealthy) and answers with the S3 website.

options.text: Add a weighted alias record for the S3 website endpoint with a weight of 0, and remove the health checks from the three records so that failed instances are left out.
options.why: When a record has no health check, Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy), so the failed instances keep their share of users.

explanation: Route 53 has [a mode of last resort](../facts/route53.md#route53-last-resort-mode-all-unhealthy-returns-answer): when every record is unhealthy, it answers with them anyway, which is why users got the failed addresses. A record with a weight of 0 waits behind the nonzero records, and the bucket already has the [same name as your domain or subdomain](../facts/route53.md#route53-s3-website-bucket-name-must-match).
takeaway: A weighted record with a weight of 0 answers when every nonzero weighted record is unhealthy.
twin: If the stem said "each weighted record has no health check" instead: first add a health check to each record, because Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy) when a record has none.

stem: A company runs a TCP service on six Amazon EC2 instances across two Availability Zones in one Region. Clients connect to service.example.com, which is in a Route 53 public hosted zone. New connections must be spread evenly across the healthy instances. When an instance fails, it must stop receiving new connections at once, also from clients that cached a DNS answer earlier. Which solution will provide a highly available design with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: spread evenly across the healthy instances
also from clients that cached a DNS answer earlier

options.text: Create a multivalue answer record for each instance under service.example.com, and associate a Route 53 health check with each of the six records.
options.why: Multivalue answer routing [returns only values for healthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-purpose-not-lb-substitute), but AWS says [this isn't a substitute for a load balancer](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-purpose-not-lb-substitute): cached answers keep a failed address.

options.text: Run open-source proxy software on two EC2 instances in different Availability Zones to spread connections and check the six instances, with a record for each proxy.
options.why: It works, but the proxy instances are software that the team patches, scales and monitors, which a managed load balancer avoids.

options.text: Create a Network Load Balancer with the six instances as targets in both Availability Zones, and an alias record for service.example.com that points to it.
options.why: Clients reach the instances through the load balancer: when an instance fails, [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume), whatever the clients cached.

options.text: Create one simple A record for service.example.com that lists the IP addresses of all six instances, so that each client picks one address at random.
options.why: Route 53 returns the values [to the recursive resolver in random order](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-routing-multiple-values-random-order-no-health-check), and [they are not health checked](../facts/route53.md#route53-simple-routing-multiple-values-random-order-no-health-check), so clients keep picking failed instances.
options.misconception: believes that Route 53 leaves failed addresses out of a simple record with several values

explanation: A Network Load Balancer spreads TCP connections across healthy targets, and when a target fails, [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume). Clients connect to the load balancer, so an answer that a resolver cached [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) still leads to healthy instances.
takeaway: Multivalue answer routing is not a load balancer; to take failed instances out at once, use Elastic Load Balancing.
twin: If the stem said "clients need several healthy addresses and the company wants no load balancer" instead: multivalue answer records, because they return [up to eight healthy records](../facts/route53.md#route53-multivalue-up-to-eight-healthy).

stem: A company uses failover records in a Route 53 private hosted zone for an internal API. The primary record is an A record for the API, which runs on Amazon EC2 instances that have only private IP addresses. The secondary record points to a standby copy of the API. Route 53 must fail over to the secondary record when the primary API stops working. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: when the primary API stops working

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch metric that reflects the health of the primary API, and create a CloudWatch alarm that watches that metric.
options.why: The metric and its alarm judge the API from inside AWS, so the instances need no public address and no inbound path.

options.text: Create a Route 53 HTTP health check that sends requests to the private IP address of one primary instance, and associate it with the primary record.
options.why: [Route 53 cannot check the health of endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-cannot-check-private-ip-ranges) whose IP address is in [local, private, nonroutable, or multicast ranges](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-cannot-check-private-ip-ranges).

options.text: Add the IP ranges of the Route 53 health checkers to the security group of the primary instances, so that the health checkers can reach the API.
options.why: The [health checkers are outside the VPC](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-checkers-outside-vpc-need-public-ip), so a security group rule gives them no path to instances that have no public IP address.
options.misconception: believes that a security group rule lets the health checkers reach a private IP address

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the state of the CloudWatch alarm, and associate that health check with the primary record.
options.why: A health check [based on the data stream for the alarm](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check) turns unhealthy with the alarm, and Route 53 then answers with the secondary record.

options.text: Assign public IP addresses to the primary instances, allow the health checker IP ranges in their security group, and check those public addresses.
options.why: It works, because for an IP check you [must assign a public IP address](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-checkers-outside-vpc-need-public-ip), but public addresses expose the API, which the alarm-based check avoids.

explanation: Route 53 [health checkers are outside the VPC](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-checkers-outside-vpc-need-public-ip), so they cannot reach a private address. For instances with only private IP addresses, AWS documents a [CloudWatch metric, associate an alarm with the metric](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check) and a health check [based on the data stream for the alarm](../facts/route53.md#route53-hc-private-endpoint-cloudwatch-alarm-health-check).
takeaway: For a private endpoint, base the Route 53 health check on a CloudWatch alarm, not on the private IP address.
twin: If the stem said "the primary record is an alias record for an internal Application Load Balancer" instead: for that resource AWS says to [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check) on the record.

stem: A company runs the same stateless web application in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. The application has users around the world. The company hosts its DNS records in a Route 53 public hosted zone. Because of a data residency rule, users in Europe must be served from eu-west-1, and all other users from us-east-1. Which routing configuration for www.example.com will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: users in Europe must be served from eu-west-1

options.text: Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record in each Region, with Evaluate Target Health turned on for both records.
options.why: Latency-based routing uses [latency data taken over a period of time](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-changes-over-time), so a European user can reach us-east-1 when that Region measures faster for the user.
options.misconception: believes that latency-based routing keeps users in Europe in eu-west-1 because that Region is closer

options.text: Geolocation alias records: a Europe record that points to the eu-west-1 load balancer, and a Default record for the us-east-1 load balancer.
options.why: With geolocation routing, each user location [always goes to the same endpoint](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-use-cases), so queries from Europe get eu-west-1 and the Default record answers everyone else.

options.text: Weighted alias records for the two load balancers with equal weights, so that each Region receives half of the DNS queries for the name.
options.why: Weights split queries among [multiple resources in proportions that you specify](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-weighted-routing-proportions), whatever the location of the user, so half of the European users reach us-east-1.
options.misconception: believes that weighted routing can keep the users of one place in one Region

options.text: IP-based records with a CIDR collection that the team keeps current with the client IP ranges that each of the two Regions must serve.
options.why: It can work, but the team maintains the client IP ranges of Europe by hand; IP-based routing suits users [from certain ISPs to specific endpoints](../facts/route53.md#route53-ip-based-routing-use-cases).

explanation: A data residency rule ties a place to a Region, so the location of the user decides. Geolocation routing sends traffic [based on the location of your users](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-geolocation-routing-user-location), and the Default record [handles both queries from unmapped IP addresses](../facts/route53.md#route53-geolocation-default-record-handles-unmapped) and the queries from places outside Europe.
takeaway: A rule about where users are served is a geolocation question, with a Default record for everyone else.
twin: If the stem said "Each user must be served from the Region that gives that user the lowest latency" instead: latency records, because they route traffic to [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region).

stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer in us-east-1. A copy of the application runs the same way in us-west-2. A failed instance must be replaced automatically. When the whole application in us-east-1 fails, users must be sent to us-west-2. Which solution will provide a highly available design with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: A failed instance must be replaced automatically
When the whole application in us-east-1 fails

options.text: Create a Route 53 health check for each instance, so that Route 53 replaces a failed instance and sends users to us-west-2 when every check fails.
options.why: A Route 53 health check changes DNS answers: [Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record](../facts/route53.md#route53-dns-failover-routes-traffic-away-from-unhealthy-record), but nothing in Route 53 replaces an instance.

options.text: Turn on ELB health checks for both Auto Scaling groups, so that the us-east-1 load balancer sends users to us-west-2 when all of its targets fail.
options.why: A load balancer acts on its own targets: [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume), and the DNS answer that sends users to us-east-1 stays the same.
options.misconception: believes that a load balancer sends users to another Region when all of its targets fail

options.text: Turn on ELB health checks for both Auto Scaling groups, and run a scheduled script that points the record to us-west-2 when the us-east-1 load balancer fails.
options.why: It works, but the team writes, runs and tests the script, and failover records with Evaluate Target Health switch without any code.

options.text: Turn on ELB health checks for both Auto Scaling groups, and create failover alias records for the two load balancers with Evaluate Target Health on the primary.
options.why: With ELB health checks, [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and the failover records answer with us-west-2 when the primary load balancer is unhealthy.

explanation: Each health check changes a different thing. With ELB health checks on the group, [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace). For the Region, [setting Evaluate target health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) on the primary alias record lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk).
takeaway: Auto Scaling replaces instances, a load balancer avoids failed targets, and Route 53 moves users between Regions.
twin: If the stem said "both Regions must serve users at the same time" instead: latency or weighted alias records with Evaluate Target Health, because Route 53 then answers [a DNS query using any healthy record](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-active-failover-definition).

stem: A company has a Route 53 public hosted zone for example.com with records for www.example.com and api.example.com. The company creates a private hosted zone named example.com, associates it with its production VPC, and adds a record for db.example.com. Currently, instances in the VPC resolve db.example.com but not api.example.com, so calls to the public API fail. The name db.example.com must stay private and must not change. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: must stay private and must not change

options.text: Create api.example.com and the other public names that the instances use in the private hosted zone, with the same values as the public records.
options.why: Route 53 VPC Resolver answers [based on the most specific match](../facts/route53.md#route53-overlap-public-private-most-specific-match), and the private zone then holds api.example.com while db.example.com stays private.

options.text: Set the VPC attributes enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames to true, so that names missing from the private hosted zone are answered from the public hosted zone.
options.why: A matching private zone with no record for the name means [it returns NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain) to the client](../facts/route53.md#route53-matching-phz-no-record-returns-nxdomain), whatever the VPC attributes are.

options.text: Create an outbound Resolver endpoint and a forwarding rule for example.com that sends the DNS queries of the VPC to a public DNS resolver on the internet.
options.why: [The VPC Resolver rule takes precedence](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-rule-beats-phz-same-name) over the private zone [for the same domain name](../facts/route53.md#route53-resolver-rule-beats-phz-same-name), so db.example.com would go to public DNS and stop resolving.
options.misconception: believes that a forwarding rule fills in the names that the private hosted zone lacks

options.text: Run DNS forwarder software on EC2 instances that answers db.example.com from a local zone file and forwards all other names to public DNS resolvers.
options.why: It works, but the team then runs, patches and scales the forwarder instances and keeps a second copy of db.example.com.

explanation: A private zone matches when it is a [parent of the domain name in the request](../facts/route53.md#route53-phz-parent-zone-counts-as-match), so example.com matches api.example.com. With no record for that name, Route 53 VPC Resolver [doesn't forward the request to a public DNS](../facts/route53.md#route53-matching-phz-no-record-returns-nxdomain) resolver. In split-view DNS, each zone needs its own records.
takeaway: A private hosted zone that matches a name hides the public zone of that name, so copy the public records you need.
twin: If the stem said "the private hosted zone is named db.example.com" instead: change nothing, because that zone is not a [parent of the domain name in the request](../facts/route53.md#route53-phz-parent-zone-counts-as-match) api.example.com.

stem: An application runs in us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1 behind an Application Load Balancer in each Region. Both Regions must serve users at all times. Each user must reach the Region with the lowest latency, and users must leave a Region whose application fails. The company wants a highly available cross-Region design that the team can run with little effort. Which Route 53 configuration is the MOST operationally efficient?
keywords: Both Regions must serve users at all times
the Region with the lowest latency
users must leave a Region whose application fails

options.text: Failover alias records for the two load balancers, with us-east-1 as the primary, ap-southeast-1 as the secondary, and Evaluate Target Health turned on.
options.why: Route 53 [includes only the healthy primary resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-passive-only-healthy-primary-then-secondary), so ap-southeast-1 serves no users as long as us-east-1 is healthy.
options.misconception: believes that failover records keep both Regions serving users

options.text: Latency A records that hold the current IP addresses of each load balancer, with no health checks, because Route 53 skips a Region that stops answering.
options.why: When a record has no health check, Route 53 [always considers it healthy](../facts/route53.md#route53-record-without-health-check-always-healthy), and the copied addresses go stale when the load balancer scales.

options.text: Latency alias records for the two load balancers, one record for each Region, with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes on both records.
options.why: Each latency record serves its Region, and Evaluate Target Health takes a Region out of the answers when its load balancer has no healthy targets.

options.text: Latency alias records for the two load balancers, and a Route 53 HTTP health check of each load balancer that is associated with its record.
options.why: It works, but for these resources AWS says to [set Evaluate Target Health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-alias-to-aws-use-evaluate-target-health-not-health-check) instead of creating health checks to manage.

explanation: Both Regions active is active-active failover: [all the records that have the same name](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-active-failover-definition) stay active unless they are unhealthy. Latency records pick [the Region that provides the best latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-choose-latency-routing-best-latency-region), and [setting Evaluate target health to Yes](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) lets Route 53 [route traffic away from unhealthy resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-evaluate-target-health-benefit-for-elb-beanstalk) without extra health checks.
takeaway: Active-active across Regions with the lowest latency: latency alias records with Evaluate Target Health on every record.
twin: If the stem said "ap-southeast-1 must serve users only after us-east-1 fails" instead: failover alias records, because Route 53 then [begins to include only the healthy secondary resources](../facts/route53.md#route53-active-passive-only-healthy-primary-then-secondary) when the primary fails.

stem: A company uses a shared-services account to centrally manage a private hosted zone named internal.example.com. One VPC in a separate workload account must resolve the records of that zone, and the records must stay private. In the Route 53 console of the shared-services account, an engineer tries to associate the zone with the workload VPC but cannot find the VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: One VPC in a separate workload account

options.text: Create a VPC peering connection between a VPC in the shared-services account and the workload VPC, so that the workload VPC can query the private hosted zone.
options.why: A private hosted zone will [only return these records when queried from within](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-private-zone-answers-only-from-associated-vpcs) associated VPCs, and peering associates nothing.
options.misconception: believes that a network path to a VPC of the zone's account lets another VPC use the private hosted zone

options.text: Authorize the association from the shared-services account with the AWS CLI, associate the VPC with the zone from the workload account, and then delete the authorization.
options.why: The two steps connect the VPC directly to the zone, and deleting the authorization later [does not affect the association](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-delete-authorization-recommended).

options.text: Create a copy of the private hosted zone in the workload account, associate the copy with the workload VPC, and sync the records with a scheduled script.
options.why: It works, but a second zone and a sync script are more to run than one association, and the two copies can drift apart.

options.text: Replace the private hosted zone with a public hosted zone that has the same records, so that the workload VPC can resolve the names without an association.
options.why: A public hosted zone answers queries from anyone on the internet, which breaks the requirement that the records stay private.
options.misconception: believes that a public hosted zone is a good way to share internal names between accounts

explanation: For a VPC of another account, [you first must authorize the association](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console), and [you can't use the AWS console](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console) for it, which is why the VPC is missing. [Using the account that created the hosted zone](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-auth-by-hosted-zone-account), you authorize. [Using the account that created the VPC, associate](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-auth-by-hosted-zone-account) the VPC with the zone.
takeaway: A private hosted zone and a VPC in different accounts need an authorization, then an association, through the CLI or API.
twin: If the stem said "the workload VPC is in the shared-services account" instead: associate the VPC in the console, because [you first must authorize the association](../facts/route53.md#route53-cross-account-association-needs-authorization-no-console) only for a VPC of another account.
